prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

FARGO, North Dakota (CNN)  -- Forecasters issued flash flood warnings for Bismarck and surrounding areas Wednesday, as volunteers rushed to fill sandbags ahead of expected record floods in the flat state of North Dakota. Explosives are set off in the Missouri River on Wednesday to break up ice jams. Areas of three counties -- Morton, Emmons and Burleigh, which includes the North Dakota capital of Bismarck -- were under a flash flood warning until 12:30 p.m. CT (1:30 p.m. ET), the National Weather Service said. In an effort to alleviate the flooding, demolition crews blew up an ice jam Wednesday evening south of  Bismarck, according to CNN affiliate KXMB. Mayor John Warford said that water appeared to be moving more freely in the Missouri River after the explosives were set off, KXMB reported. The plan is make sure water continues flow through the river channel and not spread out over land. Ice jams in rivers have been a major factor in the flooding there. Most of the state, which endured a particularly harsh winter, remained under a flood warning Wednesday, with forecasters predicting possibly record flood levels on several rivers. Snow, which continued to fall Wednesday, complicated preparations, city officials said. "I woke up this morning and looked outside, I guess I thought of the same thing everybody else did. ... [What] came to mind is what a revolting development this is," said Mark Voxland, the mayor of Moorhead, Minnesota, a city just outside of Fargo.  Watch flooded fields of snow » . More than 1,000 people were evacuated from an area near Bismarck on Tuesday night as the Missouri River flooded, Rick Robinson of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services said Wednesday.  See a map of the affected area » . Emergency officials said they were particularly concerned about the Red River, which snakes through eastern portions of North and South Dakota and western Minnesota. The river is expected to crest between 39 and 41 feet in Fargo on Friday, according to Cecily Fong of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services. The record for the Red River at Fargo was set in 1897 at 40.1 feet, according to Pat Slattery of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The threat of flooding prompted authorities to ask for volunteers to fill sandbags either to build temporary dikes or to bolster existing ones. In some areas, even at 3:30 a.m., hundreds of volunteers packed into individual sandbagging centers, an organizer said.  See images of flooding, preparation » . "There have been so many volunteers that we had to turn people away," said Ryan McEwan, a supervisor at one volunteer coordinating center. "It is very busy. They are filling sandbags as fast as they can." As of late Tuesday, Fargo residents and out-of-town volunteers had filled more than 1 million sandbags out of the needed 2 million. Fargo Deputy Mayor Tim Mahoney said he hoped that goal would be met by Thursday. Fargo's mayor, Dennis Walaker, said Wednesday that his city was about 95 percent prepared for the flooding, which is expected later in the week. "I went and looked at the dikes this morning, and they're significant, absolutely significant," he said in a briefing Wednesday morning. However, he said, "We have some areas we need to shore up." Just south of Fargo, authorities said they had rescued several people in Oxbow, a town of about 238 people, after a residential dike gave way. In some places, water had reached halfway up residents' basement stairs, and in others, it had reached the main level of homes, Sgt. Gail Wichmann said. CNN's Chris Welch contributed to this report.

outputs.L2:
**FARGO, North Dakota (CNN)** — Flash-flood alerts were issued Wednesday for Bismarck and nearby communities as volunteers hurried to prepare sandbags for what forecasters said could be record-breaking flooding across North Dakota’s flat terrain.

Explosives were used Wednesday to clear ice blockages in the Missouri River. The National Weather Service placed parts of Morton, Emmons and Burleigh counties—including Bismarck, the state capital—under a flash-flood warning through 12:30 p.m. Central Time, or 1:30 p.m. Eastern.

CNN affiliate KXMB reported that demolition teams detonated explosives Wednesday evening to break apart an ice jam south of Bismarck and reduce flooding. Mayor John Warford said the Missouri River seemed to flow more easily after the blast. The objective was to keep the water moving within the river channel rather than spilling across the surrounding land.

River ice jams have contributed substantially to the flooding. Following an especially severe winter, most of North Dakota remained under flood warnings Wednesday. Forecasters said several rivers could rise to record levels.

City officials said continuing snowfall on Wednesday made flood preparations more difficult.

“When I got up this morning and saw what it looked like outside, I imagine I reacted like everyone else,” said Mark Voxland, mayor of Moorhead, Minnesota, just outside Fargo. “What occurred to me was: What a revolting development this is.”

Images showed snow-covered fields inundated by floodwater.

More than 1,000 residents near Bismarck were forced to leave their homes Tuesday night after the Missouri River overflowed, according to Rick Robinson of the North Dakota Department of Emergency Services.

Emergency personnel were especially worried about the Red River, which winds through eastern North Dakota and South Dakota as well as western Minnesota. Cecily Fong, also with the state Department of Emergency Services, said the river was forecast to crest in Fargo on Friday at between 39 and 41 feet.

Pat Slattery of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said Fargo’s Red River record was 40.1 feet, established in 1897.

Because of the flood danger, officials appealed for volunteers to fill sandbags for new temporary levees and to reinforce existing barriers. An organizer said hundreds of people crowded into individual sandbagging sites in some locations, even at 3:30 a.m.

“The volunteer response has been so large that we’ve had to send some people home,” said Ryan McEwan, who supervised one volunteer coordination center. “The site is extremely busy, and people are filling bags as quickly as possible.”

By late Tuesday, Fargo residents and volunteers from elsewhere had completed more than 1 million of the 2 million sandbags required. Deputy Mayor Tim Mahoney said he hoped the full target would be reached by Thursday.

Mayor Dennis Walaker said Wednesday that Fargo was roughly 95 percent ready for the flooding expected later in the week.

“I inspected the dikes this morning, and they are substantial—absolutely substantial,” he said during a Wednesday morning briefing. Still, he added, some sections required additional reinforcement.

South of Fargo, officials said several people had been rescued in Oxbow, a community of approximately 238 residents, after a dike protecting homes failed. Sgt. Gail Wichmann said floodwater had risen halfway up basement stairways in some houses and reached the main floors of others.

CNN’s Chris Welch contributed to the report.
outputs.L3:
North Dakota prepared for potentially record-breaking flooding as flash flood warnings were issued for Bismarck and parts of Morton, Emmons, and Burleigh counties. South of Bismarck, demolition crews used explosives to break apart an ice jam on the Missouri River, allowing water to move more freely through the river channel and reducing pressure caused by backed-up flows.

Flood-control efforts across the state were complicated by additional ice jams, continued snowfall, and the lingering effects of a harsh winter. Near Bismarck, more than 1,000 people were evacuated after the Missouri River overflowed its banks. Officials were particularly concerned about conditions along the Red River, which was expected to crest in Fargo on Friday at between 39 and 41 feet.
outputs.L4:
North Dakota was confronting a growing flood emergency as rapid snowmelt, heavy runoff, and ice-choked rivers threatened communities across the state. Flash flooding had already affected numerous areas, prompting evacuations and an extensive volunteer effort to protect homes, businesses, and public infrastructure.

Along the Missouri River near Bismarck, demolition crews used explosives to break apart ice jams that were obstructing the river and forcing water into nearby neighborhoods. The blasts appeared to open channels through the ice and improve the flow of water. Officials continued to monitor the river, however, warning that shifting ice could create new blockages or cause water levels to change quickly.

Elsewhere, residents and volunteers worked to fill and place sandbags as rivers continued rising. Emergency crews assisted people in threatened areas, while local authorities urged residents to follow evacuation orders and remain alert for rapidly changing conditions. Snow still covering much of the state added to the danger because warmer temperatures could release additional water into already swollen rivers.

The most serious concern centered on Fargo and the Red River. Forecasters projected that the river could crest between 39 and 41 feet, a level that could approach or exceed previous records and place large sections of the metropolitan area at risk. Preparations intensified as the forecast became more alarming, with volunteers building temporary barriers and officials planning for the possibility of widespread inundation.

Although the effort to clear the Missouri River ice jams offered some relief near Bismarck, the statewide threat remained severe. Continued snowmelt, unstable ice, and potentially record river levels meant that North Dakota faced days of uncertainty, with emergency officials emphasizing that conditions could worsen before the waters began to recede.
outputs.L5:
## Fargo, North Dakota

Fargo is the largest city in North Dakota and a major cultural, educational, and economic center of the Upper Midwest. Located along the Red River on the eastern edge of the state, Fargo forms a metropolitan area with neighboring Moorhead, Minnesota.

Founded in the 19th century and named after William G. Fargo, co-founder of Wells Fargo, the city developed as an important railroad and agricultural hub. Today, Fargo has a diverse economy that includes healthcare, education, technology, manufacturing, and financial services.

The city is home to North Dakota State University, known for its research programs and successful athletics. Visitors can explore attractions such as the Fargo Air Museum, the Plains Art Museum, and the historic Fargo Theatre. Downtown Fargo also offers restaurants, shops, entertainment venues, and public art.

Fargo experiences warm summers and cold, snowy winters. Despite its northern climate, the city is known for its welcoming community, lively cultural scene, and high quality of life. It also gained international recognition through the film and television series *Fargo*, although the city itself is quite different from its fictional portrayal.

counterfactuals.output:
# North Dakota battles historic flooding as ice jams force evacuations

**BISMARCK, North Dakota — March 2009** — Floodwaters threatened communities across North Dakota as residents, emergency crews and thousands of volunteers raced to protect homes from swollen rivers, shifting ice and record-high water.

In Bismarck, an ice jam on the Missouri River caused water levels to rise rapidly, flooding low-lying neighborhoods south of the city and prompting evacuations. Emergency crews used boats and high-water vehicles to reach residents as large slabs of ice blocked the river’s flow.

Officials warned that ice jams were especially unpredictable: Water could back up quickly behind the ice, then surge downstream when the blockage broke apart. Residents in vulnerable areas, including neighborhoods near Fox Island and along the river, were told to leave or prepare to evacuate on short notice.

Farther east, Fargo faced an even larger battle against the Red River. The river climbed above its previous record, cresting at about 40.8 feet on March 28—more than 22 feet above flood stage.

Volunteers worked around the clock in cold, wet conditions to fill and place millions of sandbags. Students, local residents and volunteers from outside the region formed long lines, passing the bags hand to hand as crews built temporary levees around homes, hospitals and other critical facilities.

The North Dakota National Guard assisted with sandbagging, patrols and evacuations. Officials urged some residents in the most threatened areas to leave, while shelters opened for people displaced by the rising water.

Despite blizzard conditions and fears that temporary dikes could fail, Fargo’s sandbag barriers largely held. City leaders credited the massive volunteer effort with preventing more extensive damage.

The flooding followed heavy winter snowfall and a rapid spring thaw. Frozen ground prevented water from soaking into the soil, sending runoff directly into rivers already choked with ice.

Even after the rivers crested, officials warned that the danger was not over. High water, weakened levees and the possibility of new ice jams kept emergency crews on alert across the state.

In late March 2009, North Dakota faced major flooding in two river systems after heavy snow, rain and a rapid thaw.

Along the Missouri River near Bismarck and Mandan, large ice jams forced water out of the channel and into nearby neighborhoods, prompting evacuations and road closures. Crews and the North Dakota National Guard used explosives to fracture the packed river ice and restore the flow. The blasting helped lower water levels, although officials continued monitoring for renewed jams downstream.

Farther east, the Red River at Fargo was forecast to rise above its 1997 record crest of about 39.6 feet, with projections reaching roughly 41 feet. Because the Red flows north, ice and frozen ground increased the danger by slowing drainage.

Fargo residents, joined by thousands of volunteers and National Guard troops, filled and placed millions of sandbags, raised temporary dikes, protected homes with earthen and plastic barriers, and moved valuables to higher floors. Schools and some businesses closed so people could help with flood defenses, while emergency officials prepared for evacuations and possible levee failures.
